{"decision":"Team meeting: LFP vs Vanadium Flow Batteries — Chair: Boss Dave
Date: 10 September 2026
Attendees: Boss Dave (chair), Alice, Bob, Eve
Artifacts reviewed: lfp_battery_research.md, vanadium_flow_battery_research.md (both filed by Alice)

Purpose
- Review the two research artifacts already delivered, identify key similarities and differences, reconcile conflicting numbers where possible, and decide the structure and required metrics/tables for the final side-by-side comparison report. Capture outstanding data gaps and assign owners and deadlines.

High-level synthesis (builds on Alice’s work; does not repeat it)
- Consensus view: LFP and VRFB serve overlapping but distinct residential roles. LFP is the current mainstream solution for small-to-medium residential storage (high energy density, higher round-trip efficiency, lower footprint, mature supply chain). VRFBs offer compelling advantages for long-duration (>6–12+ hours) and high-cycle life use cases due to decoupled energy/power scaling, long electrolyte life, and deep-discharge resilience, but face higher up-front costs, lower system round-trip efficiency, larger footprint, and different O&M (pumps/electrolyte management).
- Both documents include conservative numeric ranges and provenance notes. Where numbers differ across sources or appear inconsistent, the room agreed to standardise comparison bases (see Reconciliation approach below) rather than attempt to pick a single ‘‘true’’ number from heterogeneous sources.

Key similarities
- Both technologies are commercially available for residential/small commercial applications and have vendor ecosystems.
- Both require system-level BOS (power electronics, controls, installation) that materially affect installed costs and measured system performance.
- Both need vendor-specific warranties and O&M contracts to be examined closely for real-world deployment economics.

Key differences (agreed at the table)
- Energy vs power scaling: LFP couples energy and power in modules; VRFB decouples them (electrolyte volume vs cell stacks).
- Round-trip efficiency: LFP materially higher at the system level (higher daily cycling economic value); VRFB lower, with penalties for energy conversion/pumping and deeper stacks.
- Cycle & calendar life: VRFB vendors and lab reports claim very high cycle endurance and low capacity fade when properly maintained; LFP shows finite cycle life with predictable calendar fade and manufacturer warranties (typical residential warranties ~10 years or throughput-limited).
- Footprint/weight and installation complexity: LFP is compact; VRFB requires tanks, pumps, and more space, possibly higher installation complexity.
- Operating/maintenance profile: VRFB requires periodic electrolyte maintenance and active O&M contracts; LFP requires less routine active maintenance but has fire-safety considerations and different recycling pathways.

Reconciliation approach for conflicting data and numbers (agreed method)
1) Normalise all metrics to common bases before comparing:
   - Use usable kWh (at defined DoD) as the unit for energy capacity.
   - Use system-level round-trip efficiency (stack + BOS + inverter + thermal losses) for losses.
   - Define cycle life as cycles to 80% of initial usable capacity at a specified DoD (e.g., 80% DoD), and calendar life as years to same end-of-warranty threshold.
   - Compare installed cost on a per usable kWh installed basis (including BOS & installation) and provide LCOS runs under standard assumptions.
2) For any numeric conflict between vendor datasheet and third-party test report, include both: vendor value + independent test value, with provenance footnotes. If a clear outlier exists, flag it and seek vendor clarification.
3) When only ranges are available, present conservative ranges with upper/lower bounds and indicate confidence level (high/medium/low) based on provenance (vendor datasheet, independent lab test, market report, estimate).
4) If critical numbers (cost, warranty throughput caps, minimum system size) remain inconsistent, follow action items below to get vendor quotes and legal warranty text.

Agreed metrics and tables to appear in the final comparison (required)
- Executive summary: one-paragraph recommendation per target use case (daily cycling, backup, long-duration resilience).
- At-a-glance comparison table: 8–10 key metrics (usable kWh, DoD, round-trip efficiency, cycle life, calendar life, installed cost $/usable kWh, footprint/m2, typical vendors).
- Detailed metrics table: extended rows (energy density, power density, thermal management, operating temperature range, safety/flammability, recyclability, O&M requirements, minimum system size, lead time, warranty years & throughput caps).
- Cost/LCOS table: installed cost $/usable kWh and LCOS scenarios for 3 use cases (daily cycling for self-consumption, 6–12 h backup, 24+ h long-duration) with stated assumptions (discount rate, electricity price, cycles per year, DoD).
- Sizing guidance table: recommended sizing for a 3–6 kW PV household under different objectives (max self-consumption, backup for X hours, resilience multi-day).
- Warranty & service terms extracts: side-by-side excerpts (warranty period, throughput limits, conditional terms, O&M requirements).
- Provenance and source table: each numeric cell linked to source (vendor datasheet, test report, market study) and confidence level.
- Outstanding data gaps table (see below) with owners and deadlines.

Recommended audience
- Primary: residential system buyers evaluating chemistry options and integrators preparing quotes for customers seeking short vs long-duration solutions.
- Secondary: local government planners/municipal resilience officers considering community-scale resilience, and energy advisors/financial analysts conducting procurement or LCOS analysis.

Outstanding data gaps and action items (owners & deadlines)
1) Vendor datasheets and itemised installed quotes on a usable kWh basis for shortlisted LFP and VRFB candidate products (including BOS). Owner: Alice. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
2) Real-world installed system round-trip efficiency measurements and independent test reports for candidate products (system-level). Owner: Bob. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
3) Warranty text, throughput caps, conditional warranty clauses, and sample O&M contract excerpts for shortlisted products. Owner: Eve. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
4) Residential-scale installed cost data for VRFB systems (benchmarks or vendor quotes), plus minimum viable project size for typical local installers. Owner: Bob. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
5) Ongoing O&M cost estimates (annual) for VRFB and LFP (labor, electrolyte top-up, maintenance visits). Owner: Eve. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
6) LCOS model template and a first-pass run using best-available numbers and ranges (present results and sensitivity to key inputs). Owner: Boss Dave. Deadline: 24 Sep 2026.

Decisions recorded (summary)
- Use the normalisation rules and table structure above for the final comparison; all numeric comparisons will be on a usable-kWh, system-level basis with provenance indicated.
- Include LCOS runs for three standard use cases and sensitivity analysis for round-trip efficiency, installed cost, and cycle life.
- Present ranges where credible disagreement exists; pursue vendor clarification for any values that materially affect procurement choices.

Next meeting
- Check progress on action items and review preliminary vendor datasheet extracts and LCOS run. Proposed: 18 Sep 2026 10:00 local (confirm availability).

Recorded by: Boss Dave
